convention: Finite energy means a finite bound on $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(t,x)|^2\,dx$. The global nonexistence target uses one bound for all $t\ge0$. The finite-interval regularity assertion supplies a bound on each specified closed interval $[0,T_0]$.
differs_from_paper: The paper requires one uniform bound on the entire lifespan. Bounds separately quantified on closed subintervals do not alone give such a bound on a half-open lifespan.

convention: Velocity and pressure are functions $u:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$. A global smooth solution with viscosity $\nu$ is smooth on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^3$ up to the boundary, takes the datum at $t=0$, and satisfies the momentum equation and $\operatorname{div}u=0$ at every $t>0$. Values at negative times are unrestricted, and smoothness on the closed half-space does not assert a two-sided time derivative at $t=0$. Viscosity is a parameter; the nonexistence targets quantify over every $\nu>0$.
differs_from_paper: The paper also defines smooth solutions on $[0,T)$ and $[0,T]$ and states its classical equations on the solution interval. The global smoothness condition by itself includes neither an energy bound nor periodicity.

convention: The torus is represented by functions on $\mathbb R^3$ of period one in each coordinate. The periodic nonexistence conclusion excludes global smooth solutions whose velocity has period one at every $t\ge0$, whatever the smooth pressure. The datum is smooth, divergence-free and periodic, and it is chosen after the viscosity $\nu>0$.
differs_from_paper: The paper's convention in §1.1 and the erratum appended to Fefferman's description [53] require the pressure to be periodic as well. The formal excluded class is therefore larger. The passage from a periodic velocity to a periodic pressure, through a pressure periodic up to $x\cdot a(t)+C(t)$ and a change of frame, is an argument separate from the definition; the notes accompanying the formalization describe it.

convention: The hypothesis asks for jointly smooth $W,q$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, a period $S>0$ and $R\in O(3)$ with the similarity equation, $\operatorname{div}W=0$, $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ and a point where $W\ne0$. One constant $C$ gives $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for $j=0,1,2$ and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$ at all $(s,y)$, with operator norms of the multilinear derivatives. Pressure recurrence is not required, and $R$ may reverse orientation.
differs_from_paper: Display (1.3) has only the bounds for $j=0,1$. Remark 1.2 supplies the second-derivative bound after a change of constant and states no bound for the pressure gradient; the notes accompanying the formalization describe that bound as a further standard consequence. The paper's norm $|\nabla f|^2=\sum_i|\partial_if|^2$ of §1.4 differs from the operator norm by fixed dimensional factors.

term: Physical time and the similarity change of variables
convention: With terminal time one and a phase $s_0$, the formal change of variables is $s=s_0-\log(1-t)$, with spatial factor $\sqrt{(1-t)^{-1}}$ and pressure factor $(1-t)^{-1}$. The physical velocity is $u(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$, with $D_\mu v(z)=\sqrt\mu\,v(\sqrt\mu z)$ for $\mu>0$. These functions are defined for every real $t$. The real logarithm is zero at zero and equals $\log|x|$ for $x<0$, the reciprocal of zero is zero and the square root of a negative number is zero; the concrete dilations are zero for $\mu\le0$, so the physical curves vanish for $t\ge1$. The abstract dilation laws constrain positive scales only.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses (1.4) only for $t<T$, with any $T>0$, and $s=\log(T/(T-t))$; (7.40) is the case $s_0=0$, $x(s)=v(s/S)$. The values assigned for $t\ge1$ are not a continuation of a classical solution.

convention: The raw Gaussian convolution has the factor $(4\pi\tau)^{-3/2}$, which as a real power of zero is assigned the value zero at $\tau=0$; the convolution formula is therefore zero at time zero. The heat operator on $X$ is defined separately, with $G(0)=I$. The identification of the two constructions is asserted at positive times only.
differs_from_paper: The paper sets $e^{0\Delta}u=u$ after (2.1). The raw integral formula at time zero is not the formal heat operator.

convention: An $L^p$ element represents fields equal almost everywhere. The reconstructed whole-space velocity belongs to $L^6$, and a smooth representative of a mild curve is identified with it almost everywhere in space at each time. Derivative classes and the Fourier transform have the same representative convention.
differs_from_paper: A class identity does not assert pointwise equality of arbitrary representatives. Smoothness and a representative theorem are separate conclusions.

convention: Operator iterates, interval indices and the weights $\theta^n$, $\lambda^n$ use integers $n\ge0$ and ordinary powers. The factor $r_2^{-n}$ in the dichotomy is the $n$th power of $r_2^{-1}$, and the hypotheses force $r_2>0$. Fractional powers such as $\mu^{1/4}$ and $(T-t)^{-1/2}$ are real powers, with their usual meaning for positive bases in the stated ranges $\mu>0$, $T>0$, $t<T$. In the all-time definition of the self-similar velocity the real power $(T-t)^{-1/2}$ is zero for $t\ge T$, and no solution assertion is made there; other real powers of negative numbers need not be zero.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes its physical formulas only before the singular time. The formal functions also have values for $t\ge T$.

term: The datum correction and its coordinates
convention: The interval inverse returns $e$ in one finite-dimensional subspace $V$ of the Hilbert space $X$, together with a bounded sequence of interval curves. The actual datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$, where $J:X\to X$ is bounded linear with range in the chosen dense class; $J$ itself need not have finite-dimensional range. The product norm controls $e$ and the sequence, and controlling $Je$ also requires $\|J\|$. The exported transfer assertion chooses one nearby datum, after a dense subspace and a tolerance are given.
differs_from_paper: The paper presents the correction as $\gamma\in E\subset C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$, and Proposition 2.1 keeps one correction space for every nearby datum. The formal correction space is $J(V)$, and the quantifier over every nearby datum is absent from the exported transfer assertion.

convention: Certificate data supply functions, arrays, integer sizes and proposed real constants. The certificate condition imposes the quantified positivity, regularity, equality and inequality requirements on them. A theorem that assumes the complete condition is conditional on all of those requirements, and it supplies no numerical data. In the statement files the proof of the certificate theorem is left open by design; the proof of the same implication is supplied with the formalization.
differs_from_paper: The paper separates the analytic implication from numerical verification. The earlier box-and-ball certificate, the extended certificate with rows and adjoint fields, and the steady fractional variant have different hypotheses and must be identified separately; the earlier one also differs from the current §7.3 in its parameter geometry and norm weights.

convention: $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ is represented by $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ with $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$ almost everywhere. A smooth decaying field $u$ corresponds to $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$, and $\|g\|_2=\|\nabla u\|_2$. The velocity of an element is an $L^6$ class, equal to a given field almost everywhere.
differs_from_paper: The paper begins with divergence-free $L^6$ fields whose gradient is in $L^2$ (§2.1); the formal construction begins with frequency classes and proves the reconstruction separately. The norm agrees with that of §§2.1 and 3.1 and is distinct from the kinetic-energy norm $\|u\|_2$.

convention: Whole-space and periodic heat multipliers use $\exp(-4\pi^2\max\{t,0\}|\xi|^2)$ or the integer-frequency version. Thus they give the identity for $t<0$. The semigroup identities are stated for nonnegative increments.
differs_from_paper: The paper only uses forward heat times; the negative-time values are an extension of the definition.

convention: For $\mu>0$, $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$ and its frequency representative is $\mu^{-1/2}g(\xi/\sqrt\mu)$. The norm factor is $\mu^{1/4}$ with a real exponent. At $\mu\le0$ the defined physical and represented dilations are zero.
differs_from_paper: The paper restricts dilation parameters to positive numbers.

convention: The longitudinal projection $Q_\xi z=\xi(\xi\cdot z)/|\xi|^2$ is zero at $\xi=0$, so $\mathbb P_0=I$. A single whole-space frequency is a null set. On the torus the zero Fourier coefficient is the mean, and the formal periodic projection keeps it.
differs_from_paper: This agrees with §1.4, where $\mathbb P_0=I$ keeps the mean on the torus. The periodic space $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ of §3.6 has mean zero; the formal periodic space permits constants.

convention: The formal periodic space consists of real divergence-free fields of period one, with $\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|\hat u(n)|^2$; the mean may be nonzero. Its square-summable coordinates are $a(n)=\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|n|^2}\,\hat u(n)$, with $a(-n)=\overline{a(n)}$ and $n\cdot a(n)=0$. Dividing by the weight recovers the physical coefficient.
differs_from_paper: Equations (3.15) to (3.21) use the homogeneous mean-zero spaces $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ for every $L>0$. The formal representation fixes the period at one and includes the $L^2$ term.

convention: The formal integral cell is $[0,1]^3$ with ordinary Lebesgue measure. For an integrable period-one function it gives the same integral as $[-1/2,1/2)^3$; cube boundaries are null sets.
differs_from_paper: The paper also uses $Q_L=[-L/2,L/2)^3$ for arbitrary $L>0$.

convention:
For $	au>0$, $K(	au)(u,v)=-	frac12e^{	au\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)u]$, on the whole space and on the torus; on the diagonal this is $-e^{	au\Delta}\mathbb P[(u\cdot
abla)u]$. The concrete bilinear maps are zero at nonpositive lags. The endpoint value $K(0)$ does not affect a time integral.
differs_from_paper: This is the symmetric map of (2.3) and (3.17), defined there for $\tau>0$. The abstract formal assumptions require the singular estimate only for $0<\tau\le1$. An unsymmetrized convection operator is a different bilinear map, though it agrees on the diagonal.

convention: An ordinary real, complex or vector integral is assigned zero when its integrand is not integrable. For an iterated integral this applies to each inner integral and then to the outer one, and combining it into a product integral needs the appropriate integrability. Integrability is therefore stated explicitly for Duhamel and convolution identities. For measurable square-integrable factors the pointwise product is integrable by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes integrals in classes where convergence is established. The assigned value outside those classes supplies no estimate and does not justify an inner-product interpretation.

term: Tensor and vector norms in the kernel bound
convention: In the pointwise convolution bound the input tensor $F$ has norm $\max_{j,k}|F_{jk}|$, and the bound is required at every spatial point. The output lies in $\mathbb R^3$ with the Euclidean norm.
differs_from_paper: The paper's convention $|\nabla f|^2=\sum_i|\partial_if|^2$ of §1.4 is the Frobenius norm. Equivalent tensor norms change constants, and the comparison does not preserve an explicit numerical constant automatically.

convention:
For each $t\in[a,b]$ the formal sufficient class requires a smooth divergence-free slice $v(t,\cdot)$ with $|v(t,x)|\le C_t/(1+|x|)$ and $\|D_xv(t,x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C_t/(1+|x|)^2$. The represented curve is continuous in $X$; every slice difference lies in $L^2$ and tends to zero in $L^2$ as the times approach one another. For each smooth compactly supported divergence-free $\psi$, the pairing $\int v(t)\cdot\psi$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and has derivative $-\int
abla v(t):
abla\psi-\int((v(t)\cdot
abla)v(t))\cdot\psi$ on $(a,b)$.
differs_from_paper: Lemma 3.6 assumes only a continuous $\dot H^1$ curve and test pairings continuously differentiable up to the endpoints. The formal sufficient class has extra spatial decay and $L^2$-difference conditions, with derivatives imposed only in the open time interval.

term: Assigned values outside the analytic domain
convention: Functions are defined at every real time. A derivative at a point where differentiability fails is assigned zero, and a nonintegrable vector integral is assigned zero. In constructing a Fourier class, a derivative that is not in $L^2$ is replaced by zero, and the class is zero if the divergence condition fails; a periodic field whose weighted coefficients are not square summable is sent to zero. The conversion of a time function to a continuous interval curve is zero if continuity fails, and operators defined by a formula are zero if no bounded operator with that formula exists. In the Duhamel definition the heat flow at time $\eta$ uses $\max\{\eta,0\}$ and the bilinear term is zero for $\eta\le0$. Smoothness, integrability and positivity hypotheses remove these exceptions in the analytic applications.
differs_from_paper: The paper introduces its operators on classes where integrability, differentiability, continuity and boundedness are established. The formal definitions also have values outside those classes, and the definitions alone prove no integrability, derivative or differential equation.

convention: Pointwise decay bounds use operator norms: $\|DW\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ for the first derivative and $\sup_{|a|,|b|\le1}|H(a,b)|$ for a bilinear second derivative. For a complex array, $|G|_{\mathrm F}^2=\sum_{a,b}|G_{ab}|^2$, and in three dimensions $\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le|G|_{\mathrm F}\le\sqrt3\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The formal squared gradient integral is $\int\sum_{j=1}^3|Dg(y)e_j|^2\,dy$, the squared homogeneous $H^1$ norm when these derivatives are square integrable; modal gradient and Hessian energies also sum squared components. The profile-change bounds in (B.47) use $|A|_{\mathrm{op}}$ before the spatial $L^2$ or $L^3$ norm.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes $|\nabla f|^2=\sum_i|\partial_if|^2$ (§1.4) and uses operator norms explicitly in (B.16) and (B.47). An unspecified decay constant can be enlarged when changing norms; a fixed numerical constant needs the dimensional factor.

convention: A similarity period $S>0$ is divided into a positive natural number $k$ of pieces. Set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $L=1-\mu$. The short-interval profile is $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$ on $[0,L]$; under the orbit hypothesis the formal statement proves $a_{n+k}=\rho a_n$.
differs_from_paper: The paper's $\lambda=e^{-S}$ and $t_n=1-\lambda^n$ count whole periods. Its n is therefore different from a short-interval index unless $k=1$.

convention: $C([0,L];X)$ uses the unweighted supremum norm. Curves are evaluated outside $[0,L]$ by constant endpoint extension when $L\ge0$; for $L<0$ the extension is zero. A continuous restriction is assigned the zero curve if the proposed restriction is not continuous.
differs_from_paper: This is not the paper's weighted space on $[0,1)$. The formal construction carries the time weights through geometric rescaling and bounded sequences of interval curves.

term: Duhamel integral on a closed interval
convention: For continuous $f,g:[0,L]\to X$, $B_L(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ is a Bochner integral. The lag-zero value occurs only at one endpoint and has no effect on the integral. The definition chooses a bounded bilinear operator with this formula, and assigns zero if none exists; the compact-interval theorem proves existence under the heat and kernel hypotheses.
differs_from_paper: The paper gives the integral directly. The formal definition needs its existence theorem before its assigned operator can be identified with the integral. This compact-interval estimate does not state (4.18), (4.19) or (4.21) in global weighted norms.

term: Inverse of a bounded operator and division
convention: Division by zero is zero, and the inverse of a bounded operator is the ordinary inverse when the operator is invertible and zero otherwise. In $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$ the inverse is therefore defined before invertibility is known. The monodromy theorem assumes $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ and proves a genuine inverse of norm at most $4/3$. In the inverse-transfer statements $\|S\|,\|S_{\mathbb T}\|\le q<1$ gives ordinary inverses of $I-S$ and $I-S_{\mathbb T}$ and $1-q>0$; in the interval application $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ gives the factor $\theta^{-1}$ and the geometric propagation inverses their usual meaning.
differs_from_paper: The paper defines its full-period inverse after proving solvability and uniqueness.

convention: The formal recurrence is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$. With $\theta>0$, $\chi_n=\theta^nx_n$ and $f_n=\theta^nc_n$, it becomes $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$. A bounded $x$ gives a geometrically decaying $\chi$ when $0<\theta<1$.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes the unweighted decaying sequence. Its forcing is derived from a global source; the recurrence definition itself takes its source sequence as an input.

term: Infinite series, finite powers and real suprema
convention: Operator powers and sequence indices are natural numbers; at $n=0$ a sum over $m<n$ is empty and the operator power is the identity. Natural subtraction stops at zero, but in the finite variation-of-constants sum $m<n$ gives $n-1-m$ its ordinary value. A nonsummable real, complex or vector series is assigned zero, while a nonnegative extended series may equal infinity. A real supremum of an unbounded set is assigned zero and is then not an upper bound. Convergence and boundedness are proved before these expressions are used, as in the future-tail estimates.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes only convergent series, bounded suprema and nonnegative exponents.

convention: The counterclockwise contour integral $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-M)^{-1}\,dz$ is the interior projection when the complex space is Banach, $r>0$ and the circle lies in the resolvent set. The exterior projection is $I-Q$. The resolvent and contour integral have assigned zero values when the required inverse or integrability is absent.
differs_from_paper: The paper names the exterior projection P and later its real restriction $P_{\mathrm u}$. The linked contour definition names the interior one.

term: Complexification of a real Hilbert space
convention: The complexification consists of pairs written x+iy, with $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$, and a real operator T acts as $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$. The linked norm theorem proves $\|T_{\mathbb C}\|\le\|T\|$, while a separate linked theorem preserves compactness.
differs_from_paper: The paper states equality of the operator norms. The reverse inequality follows from restriction to $x+i0$ and is not the conclusion of the linked inequality theorem.

convention: The interval correction assertion assumes $64\|\mathcal R\|^2C_KL^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$, where $\|r_n\|\le\theta^n\rho$ bounds the residual and $\xi$ is the datum displacement. It controls both correction components by $2\|\mathcal R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$.
differs_from_paper: Lemma 4.8 uses the global norm of $e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}$ and bounds only the curve component of the right inverse. The formal sum of separate bounds does not retain possible cancellation.

convention: Local data are arbitrary tuples $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)\in(L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3))^3\times L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with the maximum of the four norms. No compatibility $A_j=\partial_jv$ and no divergence condition is imposed on general tuples. Restriction of an actual velocity records $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$ separately, as equivalence classes modulo equality almost everywhere. These derivative entries need not be distributional derivatives of the zero extension of the value entry.
differs_from_paper: The paper’s local space in §6.3 consists of actual solenoidal fields on a ball, with norm $\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(B)}+\|v\|_{L^6(B)}$. The formal target is larger and uses a maximum norm.

convention: Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. At $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, restriction to similarity coordinates records $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$. The restriction is defined to be zero when the admissibility conditions fail. It is a bounded linear map for every real pair $(\mu,b)$.
differs_from_paper: The restriction in (6.7) is unscaled on the large torus. Both the amplitude factors and the use of the inhomogeneous unit-torus norm enter the formal comparison.

convention: The periodic construction fixes $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and a smooth scalar cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$, zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and taking values in $[0,1]$. Its solenoidal cutoff of $g$ is $\chi g+\nabla\chi\times A_{a,g}$, where $A_{a,g}(x)=\int_0^1\sigma g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$. For $T>0$, $t<T$, the function $f_{T,t}(y)=\sqrt{T-t}\,\bar u_T(t,a+\sqrt{T-t}\,y)$ has outer radius $1/(8\sqrt{T-t})$ and inner radius half as large.
differs_from_paper: Lemma 5.1 varies an independent physical radius $r>0$ about the origin and fixes terminal time one. The formal cutoff estimates concern a fixed physical cutoff after translation and rescaling; their large radius depends on $T-t$.

convention: For $0<T\le1$ and $0<\lambda<1$, put $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$, $t_n=T-\mu_n$ and $\ell=1-\lambda$. A physical curve is represented on interval $n$ by $v_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u(t_n+\mu_ns)$, $0\le s\le\ell$. Matching is $v_{n+1}(0)=\lambda^{1/4}v_n(\ell)$. The corresponding heat flow and bilinear kernel are $e^{\mu_ns\Delta}$ and $\mu_n^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu_n\tau)$. Sequence norms are suprema over $n$ and $s$. Each input curve has closed-interval domain; its all-real-time extension takes endpoint values outside the interval.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses one curve on $[0,1)$ and the weighted norm $\sup_{0\le t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|z(t)\|$. The formal sequence statements do not themselves identify that global norm or retain its explicit constants.

convention: Let $w$ reduce each coordinate modulo the integer lattice to the unit cell centred at $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. For $\mu>0$, set $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$. If $g$ is smooth, compactly supported, solenoidal and supported in $\bar B_b$, and $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, then $g_\mu$ is smooth, unit-periodic and solenoidal. Its normalized squared norm is $\|\mu^{1/4}g_\mu\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}^2=\|\nabla g\|_2^2+\mu\|g\|_2^2$. At nonpositive scales the defining square root and its reciprocal give the zero field.
differs_from_paper: The paper first periodizes an unscaled compact field with period $L$ and preserves its homogeneous norm in (6.1). The formal identity contains the amplitude normalization and a scaled $L^2$ term.

convention: For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $p^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1}q(\log(T/(T-t)),(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$ and $p^{\mathrm a}(t,x)=\chi(x)[p^*(t,x)-p^*(t,a+(3/32)e_1)]$. Thus the pressure is anchored at a fixed point in the transition annulus before multiplication by the cutoff. The differential residual is $\partial_t\bar u_T+(\bar u_T\cdot\nabla)\bar u_T-\Delta\bar u_T+\nabla p^{\mathrm a}$. Its bound holds on the fixed annulus $1/16\le|x-a|\le1/8$.
differs_from_paper: The argument in §6.2 estimates a global Duhamel defect by comparing periodic and whole-space heat flows. The formal residual estimate starts from this localized differential residual and then integrates it on the normalized intervals.

convention: The spatial derivative is a linear map whose matrix has entries $G_{ab}=\partial_bv_a$: the first index is the output component and the second the direction. Its columns are the directional derivatives and $|G|_{\mathrm F}^2=\sum_b|Ge_b|^2$. A three-index derivative array has the output component first, followed by its two directions. The scalar constraint pairs corresponding columns of the derivative and constraint matrices.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes the direction first, $(\nabla v)_{jk}=\partial_jv_k$ in (7.11), and the coefficients of (B.10) are also direction first. The formal array is the transpose; Frobenius norms and pairings of two transposed matrices are unchanged, but unsymmetrized contractions need the index conversion.

convention: Fields are functions on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, with periodicity and regularity imposed separately. Some conditions require period one at every point. Hilbert-space elements in $L^2(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z;L^2(\mathbb R^3))$ identify fields equal almost everywhere; the time circle has total measure one. Integral definitions use $[0,1]$, while representatives on the circle can be taken on $[0,1)$.
differs_from_paper: The intervals $(0,1)$, $[0,1)$ and $[0,1]$ give the same Lebesgue integral. Equality of Hilbert-space elements is almost-everywhere equality; continuity and pointwise periodicity of a representative are separate assertions.

convention: The nonnegative integral is the lower Lebesgue integral: the supremum of the integrals of measurable simple functions below the integrand. It is defined for every input and takes values in $[0,\infty]$, and a real density $a$ enters through $\max(a,0)$. The conversion of $+\infty$ to a real number is zero, so a real squared energy or norm equal to zero does not alone prove integrability or vanishing. Some size conditions are inequalities between such integrals; a finite right-hand side excludes $+\infty$ but imposes no measurability. With a measurable representative, $\int|\psi|^3\le\max(n^3,0)$ or $\int|\psi|^2\le n^2$ with $n\ge0$ means $\|\psi\|_3\le n$ or $\|\psi\|_2\le n$; matrix potential bounds use the sum of squared entries.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses finite norms and energies on stated function classes. The clipping before integration, the zero value assigned to infinity and the separate measurability hypotheses are additional formal conventions.

convention: For $\omega>0$, replacing $b_i,\beta_i,\beta_i^{\rm a},V,b_*,a_*$ by $b_i/\omega,\omega\beta_i,\omega\beta_i^{\rm a},V/\omega,b_*/\omega,a_*/\omega$ preserves the physical force and the column pairings, and changes $\omega^2|\beta|^2$ into the Euclidean square of the rescaled coefficients. Several nonlinear correction implications also require the reference field to equal the approximate profile and the comparison gap and form shift to be zero; these are additional normalization hypotheses.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses the original coefficient weight. Rescaling the coefficient vector alone would change the forcing term; all the listed data must be changed together.

convention: The periodic correction bound is $U(v)=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\theta\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2$. It ignores null sets of times. For a separately established continuous periodic Sobolev-space representative, it equals the supremum over every real time.
differs_from_paper: The paper bounds every time of the continuous representative. An essential bound alone does not assert continuity or choose such a representative.

convention: The formal condition permits the positive integer $m=1$ for any prescribed symmetry set, and $m=2$ when $(R,1/2)$ belongs to that set for some orthogonal $R$.
differs_from_paper: Equation (7.6) selects $m=2$ whenever this symmetry is available. The formal condition still permits $m=1$ in that case.

convention: For supplied rows $u_a$ and real weights $\tau_a$, the row quantity is $[F]=\sqrt{\max\{\sum_a\tau_a(\int_0^1\int F\cdot u_a)^2,0\}}$, and an empty sum is zero. Under the certificate row conditions the $u_a$ are orthonormal, $0\le\tau_a\le c_0^2$ and $c_0\ge0$, and then $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. In the cell construction the rows are $r_a=\sum_b(G^{-1/2})_{ab}\tilde e_b$ for square-integrable generator fields $\tilde e_b$ with positive definite Gram matrix $G_{ab}=\int_0^1\int\tilde e_a\cdot\tilde e_b$, and the stored cell number is $c\tau_a$, with $c=3/50$ in the final system. The squared norm of $\sqrt{\tau_a}\,r_a$ equals $\tau_a$ only when $\tau_a\ge0$.
differs_from_paper: Equation (B.11) includes the factor $\sqrt{\tau_a}$ in $e_a$; setting $e_a=\sqrt{\tau_a}\,r_a$ recovers it. Generic coercive implications do not themselves impose the certificate row conditions.

convention: For a linear map $G$, $G_{ij}=(G e_j)_i$ and $c(G)=(G_{32}-G_{23},G_{13}-G_{31},G_{21}-G_{12})$. A supplied $G$ is not automatically the gradient of a supplied velocity. The background curl is computed from the ordinary spatial derivative, assigned zero where differentiability fails.
differs_from_paper: The smooth linearization in (C.2) has actual derivatives. The general formal expressions accept independent derivative fields and require additional identities to recover it.

convention: The paper's label $\iota=(\iota_1,\iota_2)$ gives integer time and azimuthal frequencies $(n,k)=(2\iota_2-\iota_1,\varkappa\iota_1)$, so $E_\iota=\exp(i[2\pi n\theta+k\phi])$; the radial phase adds an integer multiple of $f(|y|^2)$. Reflection sends $\iota$ to $\iota^\flat=(-\iota_1,\iota_2-\iota_1)$ and $(n,k)$ to $(n,-k)$. For period $S$ and angular velocity $\nu$ the rotating frequency is $2\pi n/S+\nu k$. Integer $n$ makes every finite represented field of period one in $\theta$.
differs_from_paper: The formulas agree with (B.1) to (B.6). Labels and frequency pairs are distinct objects: the general projections and some cell conditions use unrestricted frequency pairs, the represented fields obtain them from labels, and the general definitions do not make the choices $\varkappa=19$, $S=\bar S$, $\nu=\pm2\pi/(19\bar S)$ of Appendix C.4.

term: Regularity on a closed time interval
convention: The whole-space realization supplies velocity and pressure smooth up to the boundary of $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, divergence zero for $0\le t\le T$, and the momentum equation for $0<t<T$. Equality with the mild velocity holds almost everywhere in space for every time in $[0,T]$.
differs_from_paper: This explains the formal convention behind the paper's phrase 'smooth solution on [0,T]'. It does not assert a two-sided endpoint derivative of an arbitrary extension outside the interval.

term: A specified representative and an existence assertion
convention: Equality to a supplied $X$-valued orbit means equality almost everywhere in space for every real time, with the exceptional spatial set permitted to depend on time. An implication between existence of a weak profile and existence of a smooth profile need not identify the two witnesses.
differs_from_paper: Proposition 7.11 specifies the weak field and period and asserts the identity (7.62) at every time. The final existential implication does not retain that identity, the certificate parameter or the correction bounds.

term: Coordinates at the origin and on the axis
convention: For $L>0$, $\sigma=|y|/(|y|+L)\in[0,1)$. The functions $\eta=y_3/|y|$ and $y/|y|$ are zero at the origin, and the azimuthal angle is zero on the axis. Hence $1-\eta^2=1$ at the origin, the polar vector $(\eta y_1/|y|,\eta y_2/|y|,-(1-\eta^2))$ equals $(0,0,-1)$ there, and the azimuthal vector $e_3\times y/|y|$ is zero. These values do not make the separate factors continuous or differentiable; under the prescribed amplitude exponents the complete vector summands vanish at the origin.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses the coordinate formulas away from their singular sets and proves regularity of complete fields through their factors.

term: Integer exponents in the amplitude representations
convention: The origin, decay and axis exponents of the finite velocity and pressure representations, and the decay order $e$, are natural numbers, zero included where no positivity is imposed. The field conditions require $h\ge1$ and, for a nonzero azimuthal harmonic, $h_0\ge2$. Subtraction of natural numbers stops at zero; the stated degree inequalities recover ordinary subtraction where it is used. The scalar majorants for the coefficient bounds allow integer exponents, with radial factor $\sigma^a(1-\sigma)^d$ away from the origin and a separately supplied value at the origin.
differs_from_paper: The natural-number exponents agree with (B.7) to (B.9). The decay-order theorem quantifies $e$ over natural numbers only, and the integer powers of the majorants are not natural powers.

term: Pointwise derivatives and the weak Hessian
convention: A pointwise derivative is assigned zero where it does not exist, and an iterated derivative differentiates that everywhere-defined first derivative; failure of the first derivative at a point does not force the second expression to vanish there. A supplied Hessian is independent data until the weak-derivative identity is imposed. Its first argument is the new direction: $H(a,e_j)=\partial_a\partial_jW$, so $h\mapsto H(h,e_j)$ is the weak gradient of $\partial_jW$. Interchanging the arguments needs a symmetry identity. For the finite representation, $H_W$ is the real part of the sum of the second derivatives of the complex summands.
differs_from_paper: Appendix B.1 describes weak second derivatives that agree with classical ones away from the partition spheres and cones. The everywhere-defined expressions do not by themselves assert that identification.

convention: The nonnegative densities sum the positive, or negative, parts of each modal term $I_\iota$ and of the stretching term $J$. Parts are taken before summing over modes and before averaging $J$ in time and angle. Their period integrals lie in $[0,\infty]$. On the quarter plane the measure is $r\,dr\,dz$, and the reflection changes the factor $2\pi$ to $4\pi$.
differs_from_paper: These are the positive and negative contributions after (B.18). The positive quantity need not equal the positive part of the combined signed form. A finite negative part permits the signed difference, and finiteness of both parts gives absolute integrability.

convention: Real and complex division by zero is zero, and the real square root of a negative argument is zero, so $(\sqrt x)^2=\max(x,0)$. Identities such as $(r_2-r)/(rr_2)=1/r-1/r_2$ need nonzero denominators. The main certificate applications assume positive periods, energy weights and auxiliary denominators; some auxiliary implications allow any real $S$, with $1/S=0$ at $S=0$. In elimination, zero slack is accompanied by a separate equation for the eliminated source.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses these expressions on their admissible domains. Division by zero cannot enforce an equation on its numerator, and positivity or nonvanishing hypotheses are needed before the expressions are read as coordinates, frequencies, weights or norms.

convention: The reflection $R_*(y_1,y_2,y_3)=(y_1,-y_2,-y_3)$ is a rotation. For weak perturbations, the velocity, gradient and Hessian reflection identities hold almost everywhere in time and space. Some auxiliary coefficient reflection assumptions are imposed only off the plane $y_3=0$, which has zero spatial measure.
differs_from_paper: The paper writes unrestricted pointwise identities. The formal weak-field identities and the auxiliary coefficient hypotheses have the stated qualifications, which suffice for the integral arguments.

convention: Every positive ray meets the exterior either in the empty set or above a positive threshold. This leaves membership of the origin unrestricted. At the origin the reciprocal radius and normalized radial vector are zero; the integral is unaffected by changing one point.
differs_from_paper: The formal radial estimate permits either choice at the origin.

convention: The exterior estimate is expressed as the nonnegative integral of the negative part being at most that of the positive part. Either side may a priori be infinite. Negative-part finiteness is a separate assertion where needed for the signed integral.
differs_from_paper: Lemma B.6 explicitly includes negative-part integrability; the regional formal conclusion does not export it.

convention:
The generic estimate assumes separate measurable sums $W^{a}-W^{r}=\Sigma Z_a$ and $
abla W^{a}-
abla W^{r}=\Sigma A_a$. It bounds the vectors $Z_a$ pointwise and the matrices $A_a$ in $L^{2}$ or $L^{3}$. Individual identities $A_a=
abla Z_a$ are not required.
differs_from_paper: The two terms in the paper have those individual derivative identities; they form a special case.

term: Column count and complex pivot coordinates
convention: The tree condition counts indexed negative columns, repeated or zero columns included, and does not replace this count by a matrix rank. A complex coordinate is an optional real unknown plus $i$ times a real multiple of another optional real unknown; on a pivot the multiplier has square one and the present real and imaginary indices are distinct. Real and imaginary parts of each loss column receive distinct column indices even when their vectors agree or vanish.
differs_from_paper: This makes the distinct columns and the complex alternative after (B.40) precise. The raw coordinate data allow arbitrary multipliers and repeated indices until the pivot conditions are imposed.

convention: For fixed $\Gamma$, a spatial field u is invariant almost everywhere under $u(Ry)=Ru(y)$ for each $(R,0)\in \Gamma$. The class also requires $u\in L^{6}$, divergence zero, a weak gradient in $L^{2}$ and weak second derivatives with $\Delta u\in L^{2}$. The empty symmetry set gives the unrestricted class.
differs_from_paper: Generic estimates are formulated for this parameterized class; choosing no symmetries recovers the broad spatial class used in Appendix B.4.

convention: The integer time frequency of a label $\iota$ is $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$, with factor $\exp(2\pi ij\theta)$. With $\theta=s/S$ and $S>0$, its angular frequency in self-similar time $s$ is $2\pi j/S$. Physical time $t$ is a different variable: for terminal time $T>0$, $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ for $t<T$, so a constant angular frequency in $s$ is not constant in $t$.
differs_from_paper: The distinction agrees with §7.1 and (B.2). A frequency in $\theta$ or in $s$ must not be called a physical-time frequency.

convention: For a valid cell $\mathsf Q$ and separate degree bounds $d,d'$, the projection $P$ of $F$ is specified by $\int_{\mathsf Q}m(r)(F-P)\overline T\,dr\,dz=0$ for every polynomial $T$ with those degree bounds, where $m(r)=r$ on a cell meeting the axis and $m=1$ otherwise. The definition chooses such a polynomial if one exists and zero otherwise; it does not use the separately supplied basis. For weighted $L^2$ input this is the usual unique orthogonal projection.
differs_from_paper: The definition also assigns values outside the Hilbert-space setting of the remainder estimates. If no polynomial is chosen, $P$ is zero; this does not make $\int|F-P|^2$ zero.

convention: Polynomial exponents and most degree cutoffs are nonnegative integers. Their subtraction stops at zero: for example $0-1=0$. A range $0\le j<Q$ is empty at $Q=0$, while every zeroth power equals 1, including $0^{0}$. Separate bounds $deg_{r}P\le d$ and $deg_zP\le d'$ imply total degree at most d+d′; that total-degree bound alone does not impose the two separate bounds.
differs_from_paper: The raw formulas include small cutoffs that the paper excludes by separate assumptions. The classical mesh additionally uses an integer side degree $d_{0}$ and permits $d_{0}=-1$ or 0 on untested resolved modes, where the paper assumes $d_{0}\ge 1$.

term: Inverse and inverse square root of a matrix
convention: The ordinary inverse of a singular finite square matrix is assigned zero. The real Gram-matrix normalization applies $\lambda \mapsto 1/\sqrt{\lambda}$ spectrally when the matrix is symmetric; zero and negative eigenvalues contribute zero. Positive definiteness gives the usual inverse-square-root normalization.
differs_from_paper: The paper imposes the positivity needed for inverse Gram matrices. The raw formulas remain defined on singular or indefinite inputs without certifying an inverse or an optimization bound.

convention: A physical cell $\mathcal{Q}=[r_{1},r_{2}]\times [z_{1},z_{2}]$ stands for ${(r,|y_{3}|)\in \mathcal{Q}}$. Cell-polynomial fields sum closed-cell indicators, so shared boundaries may receive contributions from multiple cells. Valid-mesh overlaps have volume zero, which is sufficient for integral identities.
differs_from_paper: This agrees with the indicator sum in (B.10). It does not give a unique pointwise value from a single cell on a shared boundary, or continuity across that boundary.

convention: For $\iota =(\iota _{1},\iota _{2})$, put $\iota ^{\flat }=(-\iota _{1},\iota _{2}-\iota _{1})$. Below $z=0$ use the polynomial with label $\iota ^{\flat }$ at $(r,-z)$. Vector components in the order $(r,\phi ,z)$ receive signs $(1,-1,-1)$, and a matrix entry receives the product of the two signs. The upper formula is used at $z=0$.
differs_from_paper: This is the rule of Appendix B.1. It is a formula for values and does not by itself impose matching at $z=0$ or regularity there.

convention: An interval index counts internal breakpoints at most the coordinate. Thus the selected piece is to the right at an internal knot. Outside the partition it is the first or last piece, evaluated by polynomial extrapolation. Upper and lower half-chart data may have separate partitions; the upper branch is chosen at zero height.
differs_from_paper: The paper imposes continuity and derivative matching where required. Selecting a piece at a knot or outside the partition supplies no such matching.

convention: A coefficient selector is zero outside its finite retained range. A missing corner index contributes a zero selector for that corner. These conventions affect a finite row formula; they do not say the corresponding field coefficient vanishes or that an entire relation containing other terms is zero.
differs_from_paper: The paper describes retained coordinates and their relations mathematically. The zero extension is an additional convention for writing one formula over larger index ranges.

convention: A shared-boundary identity includes its kind, mode, geometry, component when present, degree and full polynomial-test coefficient array. Equal resulting polynomial test functions or equal segment endpoints alone do not guarantee equal identities, because unused coefficient-array entries are also compared.
differs_from_paper: This is a more specific representation of boundary identity than equality of the geometric trace functional. It is used to organize the continuity relations described before (B.26).

convention: For $y\in\mathbb R^3$ with the Euclidean norm, $\sigma=|y|/(|y|+L)$ and $\eta=y_3/|y|$. For $L>0$, $0\le\sigma<1$ and $|y|=L\sigma/(1-\sigma)$. Every quotient is zero when its denominator vanishes, so $\eta=0$ at the origin, and $L\sigma/(1-\sigma)$ at $\sigma=1$ is zero and represents no point at infinity.
differs_from_paper: The paper uses these coordinates with $L>0$ and treats $\sigma=1$ as an asymptotic endpoint of the amplitude data. The formal expressions are also defined for inadmissible lengths and endpoint arguments.

convention: In each coordinate an interval polynomial is specified by endpoint derivatives of orders $p<D$ and finitely many interior coefficients, and tensor products give the rectangular pieces. In the scaled representation the endpoint coefficients are converted with the factor $s_k^{-p}$, and the interior polynomials use specified Jacobi normalizations; keeping the numerical arrays while discarding these scales generally changes the polynomial. The conversion is a finite sum after restriction to the active finite coefficient sets. Zero scales are permitted by the symmetry conditions, and no invertibility follows from them.
differs_from_paper: Appendix B.1 specifies a basis of Hermite type and its joining orders without fixing these scale and Jacobi normalizations.

convention: The family is $W\alpha ^{a}=W_{\alpha }^{0}+\sum _{i}\alpha _{i}W_{\alpha }^{i}$. Each term uses fixed amplitude data but the common phase $f\alpha =f+(\mathfrak{k}\cdot \alpha )f^{*}$ depends on $\alpha$. Thus the fields $W_{\alpha }^{i}$ multiplying $\alpha _{i}$ need not equal $\partial \alpha _{i}W\alpha ^{a}$. For $L>0$ and $0<\sigma \chi <1$, if the transition $\chi$ vanishes on $[0,\sigma \chi ]$, then $f*(|y|^{2})=0$ for $|y|\le L\sigma \chi /(1-\sigma \chi )$, so the family agrees there with an affine combination of fixed fields. Agreement of phases is sufficient for this affine description.
differs_from_paper: This is the dependence stated in (B.9). The fields $W_{\alpha }^{i}$ are coefficient fields in that representation and need not be parameter derivatives of the whole family.

convention: The matrix-valued constraint fields $\Xi_i$ define $\ell_i(v)=\int_0^1\int\Xi_i:\nabla v$. The stored total-field target $\ell^{\mathrm{tot}}(\alpha)$ gives the prescribed perturbation value $\bar\ell(\alpha)=\ell^{\mathrm{tot}}(\alpha)-\ell(W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha)$. The representation condition of Appendix B.1 sets $\ell^{\mathrm{tot}}(\alpha)=\ell(W^{\mathrm a}_\alpha)$, so $\bar\ell\equiv0$. The vector fields $\Phi_i$ of the adjoint estimate approximate the constraint fields through their gradients $\nabla\Phi_i$.
differs_from_paper: This implements $\bar\ell\equiv0$ after (B.10). The stored target is generally nonzero; the difference $\bar\ell$ vanishes.

term: Coordinate radii of the parameter set
convention: For $\mathcal K=\{\alpha:|\alpha_i|\le\rho_i\ (i\in\mathcal J),\ \sum_{i\notin\mathcal J}(d_i\alpha_i)^2\le\rho_*^2\}$, the radii of the offset sum are $\hat\rho_i=\rho_i$ on $\mathcal J$ and $\hat\rho_i=|\rho_*|/|d_i|$ otherwise. At $d_i=0$ off $\mathcal J$ this is zero, although that coordinate is then unconstrained by the ellipsoid inequality, so $d_i\ne0$ is needed for the usual coordinate bound.
differs_from_paper: With $\rho_*\ge0$ and $d_i\ne0$ off $\mathcal J$, this is the radius of (B.59) and (7.29); Appendix B.4 lists $d_j\ne0$ among the sign conditions. The formal definition itself accepts every stored real number.

convention: The two formal conditions asserting vanishing polynomial moments of vector and matrix Fourier coefficients integrate with unweighted two-dimensional Lebesgue measure dr dz on the cell rectangle. Each coordinate degree is bounded separately. These conditions are distinct from the cell polynomial projection, which uses weight r on cells meeting the axis and weight 1 on other cells. Cylindrical energy integrals include the Jacobian factor r. Each operation must retain its own stated measure.
differs_from_paper: These two formal moment conditions are distinct from the weighted cell projections used in Appendix B.3. Neither acquires an unstated cylindrical weight.

convention: A pressure class gives real unit changes $d_c$ in its moments. To express changes of global real and imaginary coordinates using complex pressure constants, the coefficients are $(d_c+d_{\bar c})/2$ and $(d_c-d_{\bar c})/(2i)$. The latter coefficient can be imaginary; the combined contribution of conjugate pressure constants is real. A spatially constant pressure direction vanishes at nonzero angular harmonics when the symmetry order is positive.
differs_from_paper: The explicit coordinate formulas are among the conditions named after Proposition B.14 and are not displayed in the paper.

convention: For cylindrical components $u=(u_r,u_\phi,u_z)$ with angular frequency $k$, the vector $r(\mathbf e_\phi\cdot\nabla)u$ has components $(iku_r-u_\phi,iku_\phi+u_r,iku_z)$. These include the derivatives of the rotating basis vectors.
differs_from_paper: The general axis-regularity predicate admits all real $k$. For $k=\pm1$, boundedness of this angular derivative need not force the transverse components to vanish on the axis. The paper resolves only $k=0$ in axis cells.

convention: The raw time-angle pair $(n,k)$ is reflected to $(n,-k)$ and the point to $R_*y=(y_1,-y_2,-y_3)$. On the paper's lattice $(n,k)=(2\iota_2-\iota_1,\varkappa\iota_1)$ this is $\iota^\flat=(-\iota_1,\iota_2-\iota_1)$. The four harmonic majorants and two full-field majorants satisfy the stated reflection and axisymmetry relations; transport bounds are axisymmetric.
differs_from_paper: The weight permutation and sign reversal of rotating-frame rates needed for (B.17) are separate conditions. Reflection of the majorants alone does not assert the coefficient identity.

convention: The final cell correction uses inverse radial or axial eigenvalues multiplying selected highest-degree gradient coefficients. Its supplied matrix is the sum of its harmonic blocks multiplied by the velocity remainder charges; each block is identified with that explicit value on the allowed cell vectors.
differs_from_paper: The generic unweighted highest-degree matrix in the cell-energy definitions is not directly the final $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ of (B.26). In the classical cell-energy form its coefficient is zero; the weighted correction is assembled separately.

convention: A perturbation is represented by v,G,H,g on real normalized time and $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, with joint measurability up to null sets and pointwise period one. For almost every time, $G=\nabla v$ and $H(a,e_{j})=\partial _{a}(Ge_{j})$ distributionally, $\operatorname{div} v=0$ and $v\in L^{6}$. Over a period, G,tr H,g are square integrable; G has the Frobenius norm. The tested identity is $g=S^{-1}\partial _{\theta }v+\tfrac12v+\tfrac12(y\cdot \nabla )v$. Symmetries are imposed almost everywhere. The definition accepts every real S; its intended normalization uses $S>0$.
differs_from_paper: The paper chooses a continuous representative in time in §7.1. The formal condition supplies particular measurable representatives and does not require that choice. It directly requires the trace of H, rather than the full Hessian, in $L^{2}$.

convention: The weak conclusion supplies $S>0$, $R\in O(3)$ and representatives $W,G,H$, jointly measurable up to null sets. Recurrence $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ holds at every point; $G(s)$ is the weak gradient of $W(s)$ at every $s$, its trace vanishes almost everywhere, and $H$ is the weak derivative of $G$ at almost every $s$. One constant bounds $\int|W(s)|^6$ and $\int\|G(s)\|^2$ at every $s$, and $\int_0^S\int\|H\|^2$ is finite; these derivative norms are operator norms. The velocity is nonzero as a space-time class, and the similarity equation holds against every space-time test field, with integrable tested integrands.
differs_from_paper: This records the weak profile before smoothing. It includes no pressure, pointwise decay, chosen parameter or correction estimate of Theorem 7.1, and it allows any $R$, whereas Theorem 7.1 gives $R=I$.

convention: The modal quadratic form uses the squared amplitudes of the Hessian, gradient of vorticity, vorticity, full gradient and velocity in (B.16). The evaluation helper takes the full-gradient argument before the vorticity argument, with its coefficients assigned accordingly. At $c=3/50$ and with no multiplier pieces, the five coefficients agree with the formulas printed below (B.16). The full piece coefficients are specified in the formal formulas.
differs_from_paper: The paper describes the added frequency terms and subtracted error terms but does not print their complete formulas. A claim of term-by-term agreement of all those error formulas cannot be settled by comparison with a second full printed expression.
